Examples: Turning a screw, turning a tap, turning a screw driver and compass needle in the Earth’s magnetic field. 1.5.2 Work Done by a Couple Let F, F be the two forces acting tangentially at two opposite ends of a diameter of a circle of radius r. The wheel now rotates through an angle θ. Therefore, the work done by each force, w = Force × 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑒 = F× 𝑟𝜃 The total work done by both the forces = 2Frθ = F × 2r× 𝜃 = Torque× θ = τθ Finally, the work done by the couple = torque× angular displacement. 1.5.3EquilibriumFig 4.8: Work done by a couple If a body under the action of forces is at rest, the body is said to be in equilibrium. Based on the nature of the motion, the body can be in either translational equilibrium or rotational equilibrium. For a body to be in translational equilibrium, the resultant forces acting on the body should be zero, i.e., ∑F = 0. This term means that a body is not accelerating in any direction; it is either at rest or moving with a constant velocity. In other words, there is no net change in its state of motion. The resultant force is the vector sum of all the individual forces acting on the body. If the resultant force is zero, it means all the forces balance each other out.

Similarly, for a body in rotational equilibrium, the sum of the torques acting on the body must be zero, i.e., ∑τ = 0. This means that the clockwise and counterclockwise torques balance each other out, resulting in no net rotational motion. A group of forces that all act at the same point are called concurrent forces. If the resultant of these concurrent forces acting at a point on a body is zero, the body is said to be in equilibrium. 4.5.3 Equilibrium of the Rigid Bodies. In a rigid body, the position of the two constituent points remains unaltered throughout the motion.

This intrinsic quality of rigidity implies that despite the body's dynamic movement or displacement, the spatial relationship between these two points remains constant and unaltered. This coherence in position preservation throughout the motion underscores the rigidity of the body, emphasizing its resistance to deformation or distortion. As the body navigates its trajectory, the unchanging relative positions of these points serve as a testament to the enduring stability inherent in rigid structures, contributing to the fundamental understanding of their mechanical behavior.

For the rigid body to be in equilibrium, the following are the conditions: iv) The sum of all the forces (vector sum) acting on a body must be zero i.e., ∑F = 0. But F = ma ⇒ ma = 0 ⇒a = 0 since m≠ 0. ∴ a = 0 ⇒dv = 0⇒ v = constant dt Hence, the constant value of v yields zero acceleration, which is the condition of equilibrium, and the body is said to be in translational equilibrium. To elaborate further, for a body to be in translational equilibrium, it must either be at rest or in motion with constant velocity. v) The resultant of the torques acting at a point on a body must be zero i.e., ∑ τ = 0. Now τ = Iα and ∑ τ = 0 ⇒ Iα = 0 Or, α =0 ⇒dω = 0 ⇒ω = constant dt Here, the constant value of ω implies for a body to be in rotational equilibrium, it must either be at rest or in motion with constant angular velocity. 1.6 Solid Friction The concept of friction arises when two solids come into contact and relative motion ensues, resulting in the emergence of a counteracting force. This natural resistance to motion between solid surfaces is aptly termed friction.
